Have you ever noticed how the words we use can pull us closer together, inspire us, or even nudge us down unexpected paths? Sometimes, it’s not what’s being said—but how it’s said—that draws us in and shapes the way we see the world and ourselves. That’s exactly what Amanda Montell unpacks for us in her fascinating book, Cultish: The Language of Fanaticism. We’ll dive into the subtle, yet surprisingly powerful ways that language can create tight-knit communities—whether that’s in a buzzing fitness studio, a spiritual gathering, or even on the outer edges of society. Together, we’ll explore how ordinary conversations can morph into secret codes, catchy slogans, or hypnotic mantras that make us feel like we truly belong. And as we peel back the layers, we’ll start to spot the patterns: how leaders and groups use language not just to welcome us in, but sometimes to guide our thoughts, stir our emotions, or even shape our loyalty—often in ways we barely notice.
So, where’s the line between healthy community and something a little more... cultish? Is it the words, the stories, or the way they make us feel? Welcome to this journey—we’re about to shine a light on the fascinating world where connection and control meet, all through the language we share. Let’s explore together, and see what we discover.

Chapter One: The Hidden Power of Words in Everyday Life
You know, it’s so easy to picture cults as these mysterious, far-off groups—strange and extreme, with nothing to do with our regular lives. But here’s the thing: the language that shapes cults isn’t locked away somewhere secret. It’s actually all around us, quietly woven into everyday moments. You’ll find it in places as ordinary as a fitness class, a company meeting, or even scrolling through your social media feed.
Most of us never realize how words can gently draw that line between “us” and “them,” or how a simple phrase can suddenly make someone feel like they really belong. Let me share a story that brings this to life. Imagine a woman, new to a city, feeling pretty lonely and disconnected. One day, she walks into a trendy workout studio, hoping for a fresh start. The instructor greets her with a phrase only insiders seem to know. Throughout the class, she keeps hearing this unique language—special words that make her feel like she’s found her people, like she’s part of something bigger. By the end, she’s not just physically energized—she’s hooked. The language wrapped her up in a sense of community she’d been craving.
And it’s not just fitness studios. You’ll spot these patterns in tech startups, multi-level marketing groups, or even among fans of certain brands. The words people use—catchy slogans, inside jokes, coded terms—they’re not just random chatter. They’re carefully chosen to create that sense of belonging, to show who’s in and who’s out. Sometimes, this language lifts us up. Other times, it’s the first step toward something a little more controlling.
The line between a supportive group and a controlling one? It’s much thinner than you might think. Picture a parent, searching for comfort after a loss, who finds a spiritual group that feels welcoming. But slowly, the group’s language starts to shape their beliefs and behaviors in ways they never saw coming. Or a young professional, eager to make an impact, joins a company that promises to “change the world”—but soon, the company jargon makes it tough to question anything or even think about leaving.
What really stands out is this: language isn’t just how we communicate—it’s how we influence, and how we’re influenced. The words we hear and start to use can actually shift the way we see ourselves, how we connect with others, and even what we’re willing to do. Most of the time, we don’t notice when these new phrases or beliefs start to creep in. It happens gradually, almost invisibly, as the language becomes part of us.
And that realization? It can feel a little unsettling. It’s tempting to believe that only “other people” get swept up by cultish language, that it could never happen to us. But the truth is, everyone’s vulnerable. We all want to belong, to find meaning, to be part of something special. And the language that taps into those feelings? It’s everywhere.
So, here’s something to pay attention to: recognizing the power of words is the first step to understanding how influence really works. It’s not about being paranoid or cynical—it’s about being aware. When you start to notice those special phrases, the loaded metaphors, or the way certain words make you feel included or left out, you begin to see the invisible strings guiding your choices. And that awareness? It doesn’t just help you steer clear of manipulation. It also opens the door to deeper, more genuine connections—ones built on real understanding, not illusion.

Chapter Two: How Cultish Language Creates Belonging and Loyalty
You know that rush you get when you realize you’re on the inside—part of something special? Sometimes, it isn’t a handshake or a friendly nod that brings you in. It’s a word, a phrase, maybe even a goofy acronym that only certain people get. That’s the magic of cultish language. It draws you close, lets you in on the secret, and suddenly, you’re part of the club.
Picture a college student, brand new on campus, totally overwhelmed. She joins a student group, hoping to find her people. At her very first meeting, everyone’s throwing around inside jokes and acronyms that make zero sense to her. At first, she feels like an outsider. But as she picks up the lingo, something shifts. She starts to feel comfortable. She’s not just learning words—she’s earning her spot. Before she knows it, she’s using those same catchphrases with pride and teaching them to the next wave of newbies. That sense of loyalty? It sneaks up on her.
This isn’t just a college thing. Walk into any busy office and you’ll hear coworkers speaking in code, using company-specific terms that only insiders recognize. In religious circles, members might greet each other with phrases that hold deep meaning—words that would sound like nonsense to anyone else. Even online, shared slang can turn total strangers into fast friends. It’s like a secret handshake, but with words.
The real power here is in the boundaries this language creates. It draws a line: you’re either in or you’re out. If you’re on the inside, it feels warm and welcoming, like you’ve found your tribe. But if you’re on the outside? It can feel confusing or even a little threatening. What’s wild is, most of us don’t notice how fast we adapt. We pick up the lingo almost without thinking—just to belong.
But here’s something to pay attention to: the same words that help us feel at home can also be used to control us. In some groups, the language becomes a tool to silence anyone who questions or pushes back. If there’s no way to put your doubts into words, it gets a lot harder to speak up. The vocabulary itself can make it tough to think beyond the group’s boundaries.
Think about a man who signs up for a self-improvement seminar. At first, he’s inspired by all the talk of “breakthroughs,” “levels,” and “transformation.” But as he gets more involved, he realizes that anyone who asks tough questions is brushed off—labeled as “negative” or “not ready.” It’s almost impossible to voice concerns without feeling like he’s letting everyone down.
And this isn’t just something that happens on the fringes. Mainstream companies do it too—sometimes without even realizing. Maybe a business calls itself a “family” to encourage loyalty, or tosses around sports or war metaphors to fire people up. A wellness brand might invent new words to make their products sound like must-haves. The effect is the same: the language shapes how people see themselves, and where they fit.
What’s really striking is how easily we slip into these habits. Most of us don’t notice when we start using new words, or when those words begin to shape our thinking. It just happens, little by little, until the language feels totally natural. The urge to belong is strong, and the right words? They can make almost anyone feel like they’re finally home—even if that home isn’t all it seems.
So, here’s the key takeaway: being aware of how language works in groups gives you power. It’s not about rejecting every inside joke or special phrase. It’s about noticing when the words you use—or the words used on you—start to box you in. When you pay attention, you can decide for yourself what to believe, which groups to join, and which words really deserve your loyalty. And in a noisy world full of competing voices, that kind of awareness? It’s more valuable than ever.

Chapter Three: Charisma, Leadership, and the Art of Persuasion
Charismatic leaders—there’s just something about them, isn’t there? They have this uncanny ability to inspire, persuade, and draw out loyalty from almost anyone. But if you look a little closer, you’ll see that much of their real magic comes down to language. It’s the words they pick, the stories they share, and the way they paint a picture of the world that truly sets them apart.
Imagine a young professional, feeling restless and searching for some kind of purpose, who walks into a seminar led by an electrifying speaker. The leader stands confidently at the front, blending personal stories, big promises, and a special vocabulary that makes everyone in the room feel like they’re right on the edge of something amazing.
The energy? It’s absolutely electric. People laugh, some even cry, and you’ll see everyone nodding along, completely caught up in that leader’s vision.
Here’s what most folks don’t realize—this effect isn’t just luck. Charismatic leaders use certain language tricks to build trust and loyalty. They’ll repeat key ideas until they stick, or come up with catchy slogans you can’t help but remember. Often, they wrap their message in the cloak of a grand mission, making everyone feel like a vital part of something historic. Their language is carefully designed to slip past our doubts and tap straight into our emotions.
Sometimes, this is wonderful. Think about a teacher who makes you believe in yourself, or a coach who gets a team working together like never before—they’re using the same techniques. But in the wrong hands, with a manipulative leader, these tools can become dangerous. Suddenly, language becomes a way to shut down questions, to make followers crave the leader’s approval, or even justify things that don’t feel right.
There’s a story that really brings this to life. A group of friends, feeling lost after some tough times, found themselves drawn to a so-called guru who seemed to have all the answers. He spoke in riddles, mixing spiritual buzzwords with everyday talk—making everything sound deep and important. The friends hung on every word, desperate for the next nugget of wisdom. But over time, they noticed something troubling. The leader didn’t like questions. He insisted only he had the answers. The language made it almost impossible to disagree, and walking away felt unthinkable.
But you know, this pattern isn’t just found in obvious cults. Politicians, CEOs, social media influencers—they all use similar tactics. They create urgency, claim their way is the only way, and use language to build a devoted following. The difference? It’s usually just a matter of degree.
What really stands out is this: charisma isn’t just about having a big personality. It’s so much about language. The right words, spoken in the right way, can turn almost anyone into a larger-than-life figure. And most of us have no idea how easily we can get swept up, how quickly we start seeing the world through someone else’s lens.
So, what’s the takeaway here? It’s not that we should doubt every leader. It’s that we need to listen closely to the words they use. If a leader’s message makes it tough to ask questions, if it’s always about “us versus them,” or if the language feels like it’s creating dependence—then it’s time to pause and think.
Critical thinking doesn’t mean being cynical. It just means noticing the words that shape your beliefs—and deciding for yourself which ones are worth following.

Chapter 4: Cultish Language in Mainstream Culture and Digital Spaces
You know, it’s easy to imagine cultish language as something that only pops up on the fringes of society. But here’s the thing—those same techniques are everywhere. From fitness studios and wellness brands, all the way to your favorite social media influencers and online communities. The digital world has really taken these linguistic tools and cranked up their reach and power, making it simpler than ever for new groups to form, grow, and influence the way we think and talk.
Picture this: a recent college grad, feeling cut off during a long stretch of remote work, scrolling through social media late at night. She lands on the feed of a popular influencer who promises that missing sense of purpose—and community. The influencer is a pro at this, using a blend of motivational catchphrases, unique hashtags, and playful inside jokes. Suddenly, it feels like she’s part of an exclusive club. And before she knows it, she’s echoing the same phrases, sharing similar posts, and connecting with others who speak that same coded language.
But this isn’t just clever marketing. It goes deeper. The language builds a sense of identity. Followers turn into fans, and those fans often become passionate advocates. The more you use the group’s special vocabulary, the more invested you become. It’s like a feedback loop—the language shapes the group, and the group keeps evolving its language.
You’ll see the same thing in the wellness world. Brands love inventing catchy new words to describe their products or philosophies. If you’re searching for better health, you might stumble across a program promising “detoxification,” “alignment,” or “manifestation.” Sure, those words sound scientific or maybe even spiritual, but a lot of the time, they’re pretty vague. The effect? Suddenly, the program feels essential—even if the benefits are, well, a little fuzzy.
And tech culture? It’s got its own flavor. Startups talk about “disruption,” “hustle,” and “changing the world.” If you pick up this lingo, you’re seen as a real team player. If you don’t, you might start to feel left out. These words create a sense of mission, but they can also make it tough to ask questions or challenge the company’s direction.
Online, it all kicks into high gear. Social media thrives on punchy phrases, viral hashtags, and inside jokes. If you want to fit in, you learn the right words—fast. Language becomes a signal: “I belong here.” It helps you attract followers and build influence. But there’s a downside. Echo chambers can form, where only certain ideas are welcome and anyone who disagrees gets shut down.
Let me give you an example. Picture a group of friends who join an online wellness community. At first, it’s fun—they feel supported and inspired by shared goals. But after a while, they notice something strange. Anyone who questions the group’s advice gets silenced pretty quickly. The language makes it tough to express doubts, and the pressure to fit in just keeps growing. What started out as a positive space slowly becomes rigid and exclusive.
What’s really striking is just how naturally these patterns show up. Most folks aren’t trying to join a cult or become fanatical. They’re looking for connection, meaning, that feeling of belonging. The language offers a shortcut—a way to feel like you’re part of something bigger. But if you’re not careful, it’s easy to get swept up and lose sight of where the group ends and you begin.
The digital age has made it easier than ever for cultish language to spread. But here’s the good news—it’s also made it easier to spot those patterns, to connect with people who value critical thinking, and to choose which words you want to make your own. In a world full of so many competing voices, learning to recognize and question cultish language might just be one of the most important skills you can have.

Chapter 5: The Thin Line Between Community and Control
Most of us, deep down, just want to connect. We want to feel seen, heard, and truly valued. And that's what draws people into groups—whether it's a club, a workplace, or an online community. There's something really powerful about belonging, isn't there? It can be comforting, even life-changing.
But here's the thing—sometimes, the very same forces that make a community feel special can also become a way to control. And often, it all comes down to the language we use.
Imagine a parent who's just gotten some tough news about their child. They're feeling lost and alone, so they search online for support. When they find a group that promises understanding and hope, it feels like a lifesaver. People inside share their stories, offer advice, and even have a special way of talking that makes newcomers feel instantly welcome.
But after a while, that parent starts to notice something odd. Certain topics just aren't discussed. If someone questions the group’s approach, they're quickly corrected—or even pushed out. The words that once felt comforting now seem limiting, maybe even a little suffocating.
And this kind of thing isn't just online. In workplaces, schools, even our own families, language can set boundaries—it can encourage, but it can just as easily shut people down. Think about a company that calls itself a “family.” That sounds nice, right? But sometimes, it's used to make people feel guilty for leaving or speaking up. Or consider a spiritual group that’s always talking about “enlightenment.” That word can inspire, but it can also shame anyone who's struggling or doubting.
The line between a supportive community and something more controlling? It can be razor-thin. Most groups really do start with good intentions—they want to help, to give people a sense of purpose and belonging. But when their language turns rigid—when it’s used to shut down questions, force everyone to think the same way, or create fear—that’s when things can get toxic.
Here’s a story that really brings this to life. Picture a group of friends joining a popular diet program. At first, they love the support and shared excitement. But as time goes on, they realize the language is almost trapping them. Words like “commitment,” “failure,” and “success” are being used to judge everyone. If you want to leave, suddenly you’re labeled as lacking willpower. That vocabulary? It creates pressure to stick around, even when it’s no longer helping.
So, what does this all mean? Well, language is never just words. The way people talk shapes how they see themselves, how they treat each other, and what they’re willing to accept. And most of the time, folks don’t even notice when supportive language starts to turn controlling. It happens slowly, as the group’s unique vocabulary becomes second nature.
The real key here is awareness. If you pay attention to the words that make you feel included—or left out—the phrases that encourage you or try to silence you, you suddenly have more power. You get to choose which groups you join, which words you want to own, and which ones you might want to question.
In a world where the line between community and control is so easily blurred, this kind of awareness really matters.
Spotting controlling language doesn’t mean you have to walk away from every group or community. It just means being mindful about the words that shape your beliefs and choices. The goal? To find or build communities that celebrate questions, encourage growth, and use language to lift people up—not hold them back.
Because, in the end, the most genuine and powerful communities are the ones that let you belong for who you are—no strings attached.

Chapter 6. Language and the Shaping of Identity.
Have you ever noticed how the words you use to describe yourself can end up shaping the way you see yourself? Sometimes, it starts so subtly—you barely realize it's happening. Maybe you join a new group, or pick up a fresh habit, and suddenly you find yourself saying things like, "I'm a runner now," or "I'm a believer." Those words—they aren't just labels. Over time, they become part of your foundation, almost like a story you tell yourself about who you are.
There’s this story about a woman who, after years of feeling a bit lost, found herself attracted to a group that promised clarity and a real sense of purpose. The group had its own unique way of talking about things—special terms for outsiders, for struggles, for what they considered success. At first, she started using their language just to fit in. But as the weeks went by, she realized something was shifting inside her. She began to see her old friends as "unenlightened," her doubts as "blocks," and her choices as either "aligned" or "misaligned" with the group’s teachings. The language didn't just describe her experience—it started to define it.
And honestly, that’s not rare at all. Most people don’t even realize how quickly new words can slip into their sense of self. Think about someone joining a startup—they might suddenly start calling themselves a "disruptor." Or someone getting involved in activism, proudly taking on labels like "warrior" or "ally." That language? It gives folks a sense of purpose, a way to make sense of what’s happening around them. But here’s something to pay attention to: those same words can also make it tough to see things from a different angle. They can create blind spots, sometimes without you even knowing.
For some, this new identity is deeply empowering. It brings confidence, direction, and that feeling of belonging we all crave. But there’s a risk, too, when the language gets too rigid—when there’s no room for doubt or change. If you start questioning the group’s beliefs, it can feel like you’re not just letting others down, but betraying yourself. Suddenly, the words that once felt like freedom turn into a kind of cage.
Take the story of a man who spent years in a high-pressure sales organization. Over time, he realized the company’s jargon had crept into every corner of his life. He’d use sales phrases with his family, and started measuring his own worth in terms of "wins" and "losses." When he finally walked away, it felt like losing a piece of who he was. Finding his own words again? That was a slow, sometimes painful process—but in the end, it brought him a real sense of freedom.
What really stands out here is just how powerfully language shapes not only what we do, but who we believe ourselves to be. Most of us don’t see the shift until it’s already settled in. The trick is to stay curious—to ask yourself, "Where did these words come from? What do they really mean to me? Do they still fit?" When you can hold your identity lightly, choosing which words to keep and which to let go, you give yourself real freedom—the freedom to grow, to change, and to become whoever you want to be.

Let’s talk about something that’s easy to miss, but has a huge impact on how we think and act— indoctrination.
Now, when you hear that word, you might picture some dramatic scene—a dark room, hypnotic chanting, maybe even some secret ritual. But the truth? Indoctrination usually works in much quieter, more subtle ways.
It rarely happens in a single moment. It’s more like a slow, invisible drift. Sometimes, it all starts with a single word, a catchy phrase, or a story that just feels true enough to believe.
Picture this—a young guy, fresh out of college, lands his dream job at a company that’s famous for innovation. He’s excited. The onboarding is filled with upbeat speeches and those classic team-building activities. But what really sticks with him? The language. Everyone keeps repeating things like, “we’re a family,” “failure is not an option,” and “disrupt or be disrupted.” At first, all that energy is infectious—he wants to belong.
Over time though, he starts to notice something. The more those phrases are repeated, the harder it gets to question the company’s direction. If anyone does raise concerns, they’re told they “just don’t get it,” or maybe they “aren’t a good fit.”
That’s how indoctrination really works. Not with force, but with repetition and emotion. Those words become background music—subtle, but always there—shaping how you see things, even if you don’t realize it. Before you know it, your own thoughts start echoing the group’s slogans.
Sometimes, the process is even more intentional. Leaders might use loaded words to stir up urgency or fear. They might invent new terms for outsiders, so it’s easier to brush off criticism. Maybe they’ll share stories—ones about people being transformed by the group, to inspire loyalty. Or warnings about those who left, to keep everyone in line. It all creates this closed loop, where the group’s way of seeing things feels like the only way that makes sense.
There’s a story of a woman who left a high-control religious group. She said the language shaped everything. Words like “apostate,” “worldly,” and “faithful” carried so much meaning, it was almost impossible to imagine another way of seeing the world. Even after she left, it took her years to find new words for her experiences.
Here’s something to really pay attention to—indoctrination isn’t about facts or logic. It’s about emotion, repetition, and quietly narrowing your perspective. Most people don’t realize it’s happening until they try to step outside the group’s language and suddenly the world looks completely different.
So, what can you do? The answer isn’t to reject every group or community, or to stop using shared language. Instead, try to stay aware of how words shape your thoughts. Notice the phrases that make you feel afraid, ashamed, or maybe even a little superior. Ask yourself—where do those feelings come from? Seek out other perspectives, try on new words, and remember: no single way of speaking holds all the truth.

Chapter 8: Escaping the Grip—Breaking Free from Cultish Influence.
Imagine what it’s like to step away from a group that’s not just shaped your routines, but your very language—maybe even your sense of who you are. Honestly, for most people, the hardest part isn’t leaving behind familiar faces or rituals. It’s letting go of the words that once made everything feel clear.
Here’s the thing: breaking free rarely looks dramatic. More often, it’s a quiet process—little realizations, tiny doubts, and those moments where suddenly, things just click.
There’s this one story that really sticks with me. A man, after years in a high-demand group, started to notice small cracks in the story he’d always believed. He’d pause before using one of the group’s favorite catchphrases, wondering, “Does this still feel true to me?” He began reading books and listening to perspectives from outside the circle, slowly picking up a whole new vocabulary. At first? It was disorienting—like walking without a map. But as he found new words for his experiences, the world started to come into focus in a whole new way.
Sometimes, it’s a single moment that sparks change—a broken promise, a flash of hypocrisy, or a betrayal that’s impossible to ignore. Other times, it’s more like a slow drip—a collection of doubts that build up over time. But there’s something most people share: a sense of loss when they leave behind a language they once trusted. Words that used to comfort you might suddenly feel empty, or even risky to repeat.
I think about a woman who left a wellness community that had grown more and more rigid. She described what a relief it was to finally talk to people who spoke plainly, who didn’t hide meaning behind layers of jargon. She realized just how much energy she’d spent trying to decode everything, and how freeing it felt to use her own words again.
Of course, this journey isn’t always smooth. Old phrases can pop up when you’re stressed, or when life throws you a curveball. It takes time—and a bit of patience—to unlearn those habits of thought that come with cultish language. But with curiosity, support, and a little kindness toward yourself, you’ll find your way back.
And here’s something important: community matters. Finding others who’ve walked a similar path, who get just how powerful words can be, can make all the difference. Together, you can build new ways of speaking—ones that are flexible, honest, and open to change.

Chapter 9: Navigating Influence in the Digital Age
The internet’s changed so much about how we connect, learn, and find our place in the world. These days, it’s almost effortless to stumble upon a group that shares your quirks, your passions, or even your wildest dreams.
But here’s the twist—it’s also never been easier to get swept up in cultish language online. Think about it: everywhere you look, there are hashtags, memes, catchy slogans, and echo chambers that just keep reinforcing one way of seeing things.
Imagine a teenager—maybe feeling alone during a rough year—who finds comfort in an online fandom. At first, it feels like a lifeline. There’s this unique language, inside jokes, secret nicknames, clever references… and suddenly, you feel like you belong. But after a while, things start to shift. Certain opinions just aren’t welcome. If you question the group’s heroes, you get shut down, fast. What started out as playful language now feels like a set of rules you have to follow.
And it’s not just fandoms. It happens in political movements, wellness circles, even casual hobby groups. The speed and reach of online conversations make it so easy for cultish language to catch on—and so tough for anyone who thinks differently to speak up.
Here’s something to really think about: online language can shape what we believe and how we act, way faster than most people realize. A simple hashtag can shrink a complicated issue down to a single slogan. And a viral meme? It can make an obscure idea feel totally normal.
The more you use that group’s language, the deeper in you get.
But let’s not forget—there’s a bright side here, too. The digital world actually gives us some powerful tools to push back. You can find new perspectives with just a few clicks. You can connect with people who love open, honest conversations. And you can help build communities where questions aren’t just allowed—they’re encouraged.
The secret? Stay curious. Notice when the words you’re using start to box you in. And look for spaces where honesty and real growth matter more than fitting in.
I know a group of friends who did exactly that. When they realized their favorite online hangout had gotten toxic, they started their own space. They made sure to use clear, inclusive language and welcomed every doubt and disagreement. Suddenly, people felt safer, more honest, and way more resilient.
So, here’s the key takeaway: language in the digital age is powerful. It can be used to control, but it can also set you free. The words you choose online? They matter now more than ever.

Let’s dive into Chapter 10: Building Resilience—Tools for Critical Thinking.
You know, just being aware of persuasive language is a great start... but honestly, it’s not always enough. In a world that’s filled with persuasive voices and seductive words, it takes real practice to stay rooted in your own beliefs. Most of us like to think we’re immune to manipulation. But the reality? Everyone is vulnerable sometimes.
The good news is, resilience isn’t something you’re just born with—it’s something you can actually learn.
Think about this: there was a college student who got swept up in a high-pressure sales group. At first, she didn’t even realize how much the group’s language was affecting her. But then, she paused. She started noticing which words made her feel anxious or not good enough. She’d ask herself, “Where’s this feeling coming from? Do these words even line up with what I believe?” Over time, she got better at spotting the warning signs—catchy slogans, that us-versus-them attitude, or when someone discouraged her from asking questions.
Now, I’ll be honest—this kind of self-reflection is rarely easy. It can feel pretty uncomfortable to notice how much words shape what you believe and how you act. But if you keep practicing, it gets easier. You might find, just like she did, that the more you question things, the more confident you get in your own judgment.
Here’s something that really helps: seek out different perspectives. When you hear the same story told in a few different ways, it gets easier to spot which language is trying to persuade you—and which is simply sharing information. Another tool? Try using plain, honest words, especially when you’re talking about tough topics. The more you can describe your own experiences, in your own words, the less power manipulative language has over you.
What really stands out is this: critical thinking isn’t about being cynical or distrusting everyone. It’s about staying curious, being humble, and being open to changing your mind. In a world where language shapes reality, your ability to question, reflect, and choose your own words—that’s almost like a superpower.

As we wrap up our time together, let’s pull together the most important ideas from this journey.
The way we use language isn’t just about words—it’s about identity, belonging, and the invisible lines that shape our thinking and our actions.
And cultish language? It’s everywhere. Not just in those extreme or obvious groups, but woven through workplaces, fitness studios, social circles—almost any place people gather.
The truth is, we all crave connection. That desire to fit in makes every one of us open to persuasive, even exclusive, ways of speaking.
But here’s the good news: you’ve got powerful tools at your fingertips. A little critical thinking, some honest self-reflection, and a willingness to pause and notice the words around you can help you spot manipulation before it takes hold.
Building truly open, supportive communities starts with the simple act of noticing—and questioning—the language we use.
Sure, it can feel a bit overwhelming to realize just how deeply words can shape our reality. But remember, that awareness is something you can build, step by step.
We’re all drawn to groups, causes—places that make us feel seen. Next time you feel that pull, take a moment. Listen for the words that invite you in, or maybe push you out. Notice which phrases welcome your questions, and which ones try to shut them down.
Language is a tool. It can put up barriers, or it can open doors.
The connections that matter most are the ones that let in doubt, encourage growth, and use words to lift up rather than to control.
You don’t have to turn your back on every group or community. Just bring your awareness with you. Ask questions, listen for the nuances, and most of all—trust your own experience.
In a world packed with competing voices, remember this: the words you choose, and the path you walk, are yours. That’s your greatest source of freedom and protection.
So go forward with curiosity and compassion—for yourself and for others. Stay open, stay questioning, and keep building the kind of connections that truly matter.
